newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds to gain as data, Buba confirm steady rates.
newsitem.headline: Bunds to gain as data, Buba confirm steady rates.

text.p: German Bund futures will add to their recent gains over the next few sessions, feeding off a flurry of debt-positive news released on Thursday.

Analysts said data published early in the session confirmed the German economy was staging only a frail recovery, helping back up the Bundesbank's later announcement that it expected no monetary policy change in the foreseeable future.
The DTB June future reached an earlier high at 101.13, but had returned to 100.88, up 21 basis points on the day, by 1421 GMT.

With a larger than expected drop in February retail sales figures earlier, and a far weaker March Ifo business climate survey than predicted, some Bund market analysts expressed surprise that the DTB future had not managed to hold its own better.

But they said these two factors, combined with the Bundesbank's decision to leave its key rates unchanged at the regular fortnightly council meeting, had helped to underpin the market, ensuring it did not dip below zero for the session.
"The market has been a bit of a mixed bag all day," said Robert Eller, a futures broker in at ABN Cicorp in London.
"The future has been breaking up and down through this neckline (at around 101.00 to 101.13) all session and it is making players a bit nervous," he said.
But he added that he was targeting 102.27 for the June futures within the next two weeks.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, speaking at a news conference following a regular policy-setting council meeting, said he did not expect any change in German interest rates in the foreseeable future.
Tietmeyer added that although M3 money supply growth had been strong, this was no threat to German inflation.
"Tietmeyer's complacency in saying that M3 poses no inflationary danger reinforces the perception that the Bundesbank's rates will remain on hold until into 1998," said one analyst.

He said this stance was further justified by the 'fits and starts' picture of the German economy offered in the Ifo survey. The March index of business sentiment fell to 92.4 from 93.6. Economists had been forecasting a rise to 94.00.
Despite a generally upbeat mood for Bunds, the 10-year cash yield spread between German and U.S. debt slimmed to 116 basis points by late European trade from 120 at Wednesday's close.
But bond strategists said there was no reason to believe this underperformance would be anything other than short-lived.
With economic activity muted, interest rates on hold, and inflation under wraps, German debt would prove more attractive than U.S. Treasuries in the medium term, they said.
